name: Shell Textures
text:
# Shell Textures

Also called: Concentric Shells

## Overview
Shell textures is a technique for rendering complex surface geometry in real-time using concentric 3D rings or shells around a model, where shells are transparent except at the intersection with the microgeometry [S1, unofficial]. It builds on [Real-time shell space rendering](11590-real-time-shell-space-rendering.md) by applying specific texture sampling strategies to the shell space to simulate volumetric microgeometry (such as fur) rather than just solid volume [S1, unofficial].

## How it works
**Inputs and Outputs:**
*   **Input:** A base polygonal mesh representing the macro-geometry; a precomputed volumetric texture (e.g., fur volume) containing microgeometry data; spherical harmonic coefficients for [precomputed radiance transfer (PRT)](#9429-precomputed-radiance-transfer-prt.md) [S1, unofficial].
*   **Output:** A rendered image with realistic microgeometry and global lighting effects at real-time frame rates [S1, unofficial].

**Data Structures:**
*   **Shell Volume:** A 3D texture or volume data structure where the radial distance from the surface corresponds to the depth within the microgeometry (e.g., hair length) [S1, unofficial].
*   **PRT Textures:** Textures storing the object’s spherical light transfer function in a spherical/zonal harmonic basis, allowing approximate illumination in arbitrary lighting environments [S1, unofficial].

**Steps:**
1.  **Shell Generation:** For each shell index $i$ from $0$ to $N-1$ (where $N$ is the total number of shells):
    a.  Perturb the vertices of the base model along their surface normals by an offset amount $d_i$, increasing linearly with the shell index [S1, unofficial].
    b.  Render the perturbed model into a framebuffer [S1, unofficial].
    c.  Sample the shell volume texture at the corresponding radial level for each fragment [S1, unofficial].
    d.  Apply [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md) to accumulate the transparent shells [S1, unofficial].
2.  **Lighting Reconstruction:** For each rendered point:
    a.  Rotate the precomputed transfer function from its local frame to the world frame using the surface normal and tangent space [S1, unofficial].
    b.  Project the rotated transfer function back into the spherical harmonic (SH) basis [S1, unofficial].
    c.  Project the current lighting environment into the [SH basis](#5603-spherical-harmonics.md) [S1, unofficial].
    d.  Compute the dot product between the lighting SH coefficients and the transfer SH coefficients to determine the final color [S1, unofficial].

**Parameters:**
*   **Number of Shells ($N$):** 16 shells are usually sufficient to create realistic fur [S1, unofficial].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
*   **Silhouette Gaps:** Shells create gaps near the object silhouette because they overlap when viewed from above but separate at edges [S1, unofficial]. This occurs because shells become parallel to the view direction at the silhouette, making gaps apparent [S1, unofficial].
*   **Remedy:** The original Lengyel method remedies this by adding fins, which are quads perpendicular to the model generated by extruding edges outward, or by adding small textures rendered normal to the surface across all edges, both faded in as the edge approaches the silhouette [S1, unofficial]. Some implementations omit fins for simplicity, accepting the gap artifact [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### Concentric Shells Fur Rendering
A variant specifically for rendering fur by generating concentric shells around a model [S1, unofficial]. Each shell is rendered with an alpha-blended texture sampled from the fur volume at the corresponding level [S1, unofficial]. The offset between shells creates the impression of geometric fur movement relative to the camera [S1, unofficial]. It uses a vertex shader to perturb vertices along the normal linearly for each shell draw call [S1, unofficial]. It typically uses 16 shells [S1, unofficial]. It suffers from silhouette gaps where shells become parallel to the view direction [S1, unofficial]. Unlike the base Lengyel method, this implementation may omit fins to simplify the model, relying solely on the shell textures [S1, unofficial].

## Operating characteristics
*   **Time Complexity:** Linear with respect to the number of shells $N$, as the model is drawn once per shell [S1, unofficial].
*   **Memory Complexity:** Not given in the sources.
*   **Performance:** Capable of real-time frame rates for complex microgeometry [S1, unofficial].
*   **Strengths:** Realistic appearance of volumetric microgeometry (fur); supports global lighting effects via PRT [S1, unofficial].
*   **Limitations:** Silhouette gaps if fins are not used; lighting scheme may be limited to ambient/diffuse/specular if full self-shadowing is not implemented [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The technique was developed by John Kloetzli, combining Lengyel’s shell/fin method [2001] with Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) using spherical harmonics [S1, unofficial]. It allows for real-time rendering of microgeometry with global lighting effects [S1, unofficial]. The method is viewed as a real-time implementation of the Kajiya and Kay [1989] fur model, adapted for PRT [S1, unofficial].

## Sources
[S1] A Volumetric Approach to Rendering Microgeometry Using PRT, https://www.cs.umbc.edu/~ugrad/honors/theses/JohnKloetzli.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)
